newsitem.title: USA: Russian envoy praises NATO ties, condemns expansion.
newsitem.headline: Russian envoy praises NATO ties, condemns expansion.

text.p: Russia's new relationship with NATO was working well but plans by the alliance to expand eastward could be the "last mistake of this century," Russia's envoy to the United States said on Wednesday.
"We still believe it is a mistake to enlarge NATO," Russian Ambassador Yuli Vorontsov told a U.S. State Department conference on NATO.
"Don't continue the mistakes of the 20th century into the 21st century," he told delegates. "Why do you want to move the military machine of NATO to our borders?"

The 16-member military alliance invited the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland to join NATO at a summit in Madrid earlier this month. NATO's current members also agreed to keep the door open to future applicants after the first wave is expected to enter in April 1999.

Vorontsov said his country was particularly concerned about the situation in the Baltic states. He stressed Russia was strongly against the positioning, for example, of any strategic weapons on Estonian soil.
"Our reaction will be very fierce," he warned.
NATO has said it has no plans to station nuclear weapons on the territory of any new member.

Steven Pifer, a special assistant to President Bill Clinton, said enlargement was not motivated by a fear of Russia and should not be seen as a threat. "As we work together we can start to break down some of the stereotypes from the Cold War."
Despite Russia's strong objections to enlargement, Vorontsov said his country was looking forward to a positive relationship with the alliance.

He said the first meeting of a NATO-Russia partnership council on July 18 had gone well and rules and procedures were laid down for another meeting on Sept. 11 and one at a ministerial level on Sept. 22.
"The first meeting was in a positive atmosphere and one of real cooperation. We are glad that mechanisms, and very effective mechanisms, have been created and put into effect," he said.
The partnership meetings emerged after Russia signed a Founding Act with NATO in May, establishing a new post-Cold War relationship with the alliance.
Vorontsov said the next meeting would look, among other issues, at Russia's role in Bosnia and further cooperation in peacekeeping.

He praised the relationship between Russian troops and NATO forces in Bosnia, but voiced concern about the hunting down of alleged war criminals. While criminals had to be brought to trial, it was not the job of NATO forces to capture them. "It is a risky and tricky business," he said.
